## Monitoring of Chinese muntjac {#sec-monitoring-projects}

### Monitoring in Belgium

#### Past monitoring by INBO

In Belgium, monitoring of Chinese muntjac was conducted in Flanders, specifically within Park Vordenstein (Schoten, near Antwerp) and the nearby forest complexes of Peerdsbos and De Inslag.
Vordenstein hosts the longest-established population of muntjac in the region and has been under systematic camera-trap surveillance during the winter period (November to May) for four consecutive years: 2020–2021, 2021–2022, 2022–2023, and 2023–2024.
In both 2022–2023 and 2023–2024, 16 cameras were deployed within Vordenstein.
During the 2023–2024 season, these cameras were active from 21 November 2023 to 13 May 2024 (174 days), with parallel monitoring in an adjacent forest corridor over the same period.
A pool of 16 cameras was rotated across Peerdsbos (21 November 2023 – 21 February 2024; 92 days) and De Inslag (21 February 2024 – 13 May 2024; 82 days).
An additional fixed camera placed adjacent to the study areas brought the total number of operational cameras to 33 at any given time.
Cameras were active for the whole 24h period.
For use with the Random Encounter Model to estimate population sizes, each camera was positioned facing a clearly defined diamond-shaped plot of 10 by 10 meters (100 m²), marked using a 40-meter tape and four corner stakes with colored ribbons.
Prior to each deployment, the camera was leveled and calibrated using a vertical measuring stick placed in at least 15–20 positions within the plot, held for 10 seconds per position.
The stick was marked every 20 cm from 20 to 100 cm height to enable later distance and movement analysis from the images.
This monitoring project has now finished, i.e. no active cameras remain since 2024.

Translated description from d’Hondt et al.:

Camera traps were set up from December 2020 to June 2021, and from November 2021 to May 2022.
Visibility is optimal during the winter months.
The locations are shown in Figure 4.
Three cameras were set up north of the E19 motorway (Bonte Hanek Noord, BHN11-BHN13).
One camera trap was installed west of the park (Bonte Hanek Zuid, BHZ14).
In Park Vordenstein itself, six (VOR05 to VOR10) and ten camera traps were set up in the two periods (additional placement of VOR15 to VOR18) respectively.
The locations were partly chosen at random, but not entirely: with a view to control, some cameras were aimed at clearings or open spaces in the forest.
The camera traps (Reconyx, HyperFire 2) were installed at a height of approximately half a metre and aimed roughly northwards to avoid backlighting or triggers from sunlight .
The sensitivity was set to high.
A series of ten photos was taken per detection.
If the movement continued, the series followed each other without pause.
Every twelve hours, a photo was taken automatically, which served as a check for the proper functioning of the camera.
The cameras were visited regularly for general inspection and interim readings.
All images were processed using the online platform Agouti (Casaer et al. 2019).
Consecutive images are automatically collected in a sequence (i.e. a multiple of ten photos) to which observations can then be linked (of animals, with information about gender and behaviour).
The resulting datasets were processed in Rstudio (version 2023.03.1, Posit Software), using, among other things, the camera trap-specific packages activity (Rowcliffe 2023) and camtraptor (Oldoni et al. 2023).
Based on these data, we describe our observations of numbers, sexes, behaviour and day-night rhythm in the muntjac.
In order to interpret the day-night rhythm correctly, we corrected for the variation in day length within the study period using the method of Vazquez et al. (2019).
To determine whether day-night patterns differed between species, the probability that both patterns originate from the same distribution is examined (Ridout & Linkie 2009, Rowcliffe 2023; 999 iterations).
To describe the number of detections over time, we use the number of sequences with muntjac per time unit that a camera was effectively operational (relative abundance index or RAI; Ferretti et al. 2023).
This corrects for unequal times of installation and dismantling and (possible) temporary defects.

#### Current monitoring by ANB

In Park Vordenstein, the Agency for Nature and Forest (ANB) has set up a network of so-called rapid-response cameras.
These cameras are strategically placed in locations where muntjac are already known to occur and where the likelihood of detection is highest—such as specific corridors or frequently used routes.
Unlike the broader monitoring network, the goal of these cameras is not to track population trends or estimate density, but to enable immediate response.
The cameras are equipped with a system that sends out an automatic alert when a muntjac is detected, allowing a trained hunting team to be deployed rapidly to locate and remove the animal.
Images are not collected and reviewed after several weeks, as this would be too late for intervention.
Instead, the system is designed to provide real-time detection and response.
This rapid-response network is expected to be operational starting in 2025.

### Monitoring in the Netherlands

A muntjac monitoring project in the Netherlands was conducted from January to March 2016 in three main locations: Landgoed De Utrecht, Heiligstraatje Hilvarenbeek, and Oost-Zeeuws-Vlaanderen.
These areas were selected based on recent sightings between 2011 and 2015.
Fieldwork included daytime habitat surveys during morning and evening twilight, as well as targeted interviews with local residents and land managers.
A total of six camera traps were deployed across nine specific sites within these regions.
Cameras were active for 117 nights, yielding a combined 345 camera-trap nights.
Deployment periods varied by location: a single camera in Oost-Zeeuws-Vlaanderen was active from 13 January to 23 February; three cameras at Landgoed De Utrecht operated from 28 January to 23 February (26 nights), followed by a rotation of one and four cameras for shorter spans in March; and two cameras at Hilvarenbeek recorded from 23 February to 29 March.
Cameras were generally placed at strategic transition zones, such as forest edges bordering open fields.
Despite the extensive effort, no muntjacs were detected on camera, underscoring the species' low detectability in the wild and possible rarity at the monitored sites during the survey period.

### Monitoring in France

A monitoring project for Chinese muntjac in France was conducted between 2019 and 2021 in the Rambouillet Forest, located southwest of Paris.
This area is part of the Yvelines department, where previous muntjac presence had been recorded.
Camera trapping formed the core of the detection strategy, with cameras placed in two forest sectors (Gambaiseuil and La Villeneuve) across 25 locations.
The cameras were active for a total of 1,825 trap nights, distributed over multiple short deployment periods from October to April during the three monitoring years.
Each site was monitored for an average of 2 to 4 weeks.
The study employed one camera per site, and although muntjac presence was confirmed in some sectors, detection rates remained low, highlighting the species' elusive nature and the challenge of using traditional camera trapping methods for early detection in dense forested environments.

### Monitoring in the UK

Quote from the supporting document *Guidance on establishing surveillance systems for invasive alien species of Union concern in terrestrial and freshwater environments* [(IUCN, 2024, pp. 35–43)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?slw92B):\
“Cameras can be set for specific surveys, or to contribute to citizen science initiatives (see technique 3 above).
For example, MammalNet (Hsing et al., 2022) is a partnership between different scientific and academic institutions in Europe and citizen scientists using tools such as camera traps to monitor wild mammals across Europe.
The first phase of the project focused on Croatia, Germany, Poland, Spain, but projects and partners are already being incorporated in new countries, including Italy, Hungary, Ireland, Portugal and the Balkan countries.
Camera traps set for general monitoring purposes have provided the first records of a number of IAS, including the raccoon in Northern England, and the first record of axis deer in Brazil (Foster et al., 2021).
Cameras operated by hunters in Scandinavia provide a major source of raccoon dog reports (Dahl & Åhlén, 2017).”
